# Main Street IQ | Full Site Content

> Main Street IQ is financial IQ for lower middle market companies, with two lines of work. Fractional CFO: fractional and interim CFO leadership that works the decisions alongside you, not from the sideline. Wine Country Intelligence: AI advisory for wineries, built on a quarterly benchmark of Central Coast wineries and what AI search says about each one. Led by founder Scott Hess. Main Street IQ is based on California's Central Coast, works in person across six coastal California counties (Santa Barbara, San Luis Obispo, Ventura, Los Angeles, Orange, and San Diego), and works remotely with lower middle market companies nationwide. It goes deepest in two market segments, DTC ecommerce and wineries, and also works with health and wellness and elective medicine practices. Every Fractional CFO engagement is built on the RAID model (Redundant, Agile, Intelligent, Data-Driven). Veteran-owned and operated.

## Homepage

### Value Proposition

Finance teams break as you grow. We build one that scales.

We build the finance function for lower middle market companies, and we run it alongside you: redundant so it never depends on one person, automation-first so it scales without new headcount, and staffed by operators who work the decisions with you, not scorekeepers who hand you last quarter's numbers. Underneath it runs a live intelligence engine that reads your market, your funnel, your cohorts, and what AI search says about you, so every call is made on a current read. Deepest in ecommerce and wine.

Main Street IQ is financial IQ for lower middle market companies, with two lines of work.

- Fractional CFO: fractional and interim CFO leadership that works the decisions alongside you, not from the sideline. AI search visibility and finance automation are part of how this work runs, not separate services.

### The Problem: Finance Is the Function That Breaks Quietly

In most lower middle market companies, the finance function grows by accident. One person learns where everything is. The close depends on them. The reporting is a stack of spreadsheets no one else can run. It works, until it doesn't: that person takes a week off, or leaves, or the business doubles and the manual process cannot keep up. By the time it breaks, the cost is already paid. Decisions get made on last month's numbers. Cash surprises show up late. The owner becomes the backstop for a function they never wanted to run.

A finance team should do the opposite. Run without depending on any one person. Catch the problem early. Tell you what to do next, not just what already happened.

### The RAID Model

We build and run finance functions on four principles. They turn finance from the bottleneck that breaks into the function that scales with you.

- **Redundant**: Documented, cross-trained processes. No single points of failure. The function runs whether any one person is in the building or not.
- **Agile**: Automation before headcount. Systems handle the repetitive work so the people handle the thinking, and the function scales without a hiring spree.
- **Intelligent**: Finance that operates like an owner, not a scorekeeper. It does not just report what happened. It drives what happens next.
- **Data-Driven**: Every workstream owner carries three to five KPIs tied to real business levers. A current read on cash, margin, and the metrics that move the business.

RAID is the standard behind every Engage and Manage engagement. Full explainer: https://www.mainstreetiq.com/raid-framework

### A CFO Lens, Not an Agency Lens

Most market intelligence is built by marketers, for marketers. It tells you what's trending and where competitors are spending. Useful, but it stops at the top of the funnel. We read your acquisition the way a CFO reads a P&L: cash flow modeling, CAC and LTV at the segment level, forecasting, inventory planning, the pricing decision that adds margin and the one that quietly subtracts it, and which AI-search result is showing up for buyers who actually convert. The work product is intelligence; the discipline is finance.

### AI Discoverability: Part of the CFO Work

Before a prospect ever reaches your site, they ask ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini who to trust in your category. That answer is built from your whole footprint, not just your website, and if you are absent from it you never get the visit. As part of the Fractional CFO work, we read that answer the way we read the rest of your funnel: which touchpoints it draws on, where you are missing, and which fix is worth making first. For wineries, this is Wine Country Intelligence. Routing page: https://www.mainstreetiq.com/discoverability

### Two Ways That Work

The difference is not the size of the number. It is who owns the books.

- **Engage | A CFO alongside your team.** You keep your finance team. We bring senior judgment and the intelligence engine to the decisions that actually move the business: pricing, hiring, capital allocation, channel shifts, annual planning, and we hold the function to the RAID standard so the team you have runs tighter between sessions. For founders and CEOs who have execution covered and want a CFO working the decision moments with them.
- **Manage | Your finance department, run by us.** We are the finance function. Close, cash, books, investor reporting, and the CEO dashboard, built on RAID from the first close and run by the CFO with an embedded team and the engine underneath. For founders and CEOs who would rather not build a finance team at all. Run for a small number of clients at a time.

Not sure which one is you? That is the Intro Call. Both are scoped there, against your actual situation, not off a price card.

### FAQ

**What does Main Street IQ actually do?**
We build and run a scalable finance function for lower middle market companies, on a model we call RAID: redundant, agile, intelligent, and data-driven. Underneath it runs a live intelligence engine that reads your market, your funnel, your cohorts, and what AI search says about you, so every call is made on a current read instead of last quarter's numbers. Engage and Manage are the two ways to have that CFO alongside you: Engage when you keep your finance team, Manage when you want us to be it.

**Who is Main Street IQ for?**
Lower middle market companies, including small and family wineries. We go deepest in two market segments, DTC ecommerce brands and wineries, and we also work with health and wellness and elective medicine practices. We work in person across six coastal California counties, from San Luis Obispo to San Diego, and remotely with founders and CEOs elsewhere. Main Street IQ is veteran-owned and operated.

**How is Main Street IQ different from a marketing agency or a BI tool?**
An agency sells you campaigns and reports on impressions. A BI tool sells you dashboards you will not open. We sell you the CFO's read on whether your acquisition pencils out, the cohorts that compound versus the ones that churn, and the pricing decision that adds margin versus the one that quietly subtracts it.

**How does pricing work at Main Street IQ?**
Pricing depends on your situation, so most of it is scoped on the Intro Call rather than printed on a tier card. The published prices are the county edition of the Wine Country Intelligence Report, Monitor, and Monitor Plus for wineries, and the Website Audit, which is open to any business. Everything else, you hear the number once we understand the business.

**How do I get started with Main Street IQ?**
Book a 30-minute Intro Call. We talk about where the business is today, where the gaps are, and which offering fits your situation. If we are not the right fit we will say so.

## Services

### How We Work

Main Street IQ's Fractional CFO line comes with a built-in intelligence engine. The CFO works alongside you. The engine reads the market, the funnel, and your customer cohorts, so the decisions you make are grounded in what is actually happening. AI search visibility and AI consulting are part of how this work runs, not separate services. Full page: https://www.mainstreetiq.com/our-services

### What the CFO Reads, and What Runs Underneath

- **Your numbers**: The close, the cash, margin by channel, and acquisition cost and lifetime value by customer cohort.
- **Your market and AI search**: Where your website loses buyers, and what ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Gemini answer when a buyer asks about your category. The Website Audit gives that read on its own, for any business.
- **Automation underneath**: Close prep, reconciliations, cash forecast reads, and report drafting run on automation, so the time goes to judgment instead of data pulls. Every output is reviewed by the CFO before it reaches you.
- **For wineries**: Wine Country Intelligence benchmarks Central Coast wineries every quarter, and Monitor and Monitor Plus track a winery month over month.

### Three Places You Can Be

- **Reports and Audits**: Written findings, no CFO in the room. For any business, the Website Audit or Audit Pro; for wineries, the Wine Country Intelligence Report county edition, and Monitor or Monitor Plus. Each stands alone, with its price on its page.
- **Engage**: A CFO alongside your team. You keep your finance team and own the books; we bring the CFO and the intelligence engine to the decisions that move the business.
- **Manage**: Your finance department, run by us. We run the books, the close, cash, and customer cohorts, with the engine underneath and a named operator on your account. Limited to three clients at a time.

Capital raises, sale processes, lender packages, and succession planning sit outside scope; we work alongside your bankers and advisors and refer that work out.

### Engagement Shapes

- [Engage](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/engage): A CFO alongside your team. A fractional CFO on a standing monthly cadence: a monthly strategic-oversight session, a quarterly review with a refreshed roadmap, and decision support between sessions on pricing, hiring, capital, and channel decisions. You keep your finance team and own the books. For wineries, Monitor Plus runs underneath. Scoped on an Intro Call.
- [Manage](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/manage): The productized embedded finance and accounting function for lower middle market companies. One fractional CFO, one named operator, four workstreams, and a CEO dashboard. Bookkeeping with accuracy tracked on every close, monthly close signed by day eight, a 13-week cash forecast kept current on a cadence set for each business, and customer cohort unit economics. Limited to three clients at a time. Scoped on an Intro Call.
- [Interim Finance Leadership](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/interim-finance-leadership): For when a CFO, Finance Director, or Head of Finance has just left or is about to. A time-boxed engagement in the seat that embeds in days, stabilizes the function, and hands it to your next permanent hire.
- [Finance Director Services](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/finance-director-services): FP&A, management reporting, and operational finance leadership for companies that need the function but not the CFO price tag. The Finance Director seat is covered through Engage (you keep your team) or Manage (we run the function); full-time cover while you hire is an interim engagement.
- [The RAID Framework](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/raid-framework): How Main Street IQ builds and runs a finance function: Redundant, Agile, Intelligent, Data-Driven. The operating standard behind every Engage and Manage engagement.
- [AI Consulting](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/ai-consulting): AI consulting from a firm that runs on it, as part of the Fractional CFO work rather than a separate service. Main Street IQ runs its own finance work on AI, from close prep and reconciliations to cash forecast reads and report drafting, with a human CFO signing every conclusion. For lower middle market companies in Santa Barbara and San Luis Obispo counties and across coastal California: where AI actually pays back, what AI search says about you, and working systems put in with guardrails.

### Category Comparison

- [Fractional CFO vs. CPA](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/fractional-cfo-vs-cpa): The difference between a fractional CFO and a CPA or bookkeeper offering "CFO services." Covers what each role actually does, where the gap shows up, the four diagnostic questions to ask a fractional CFO candidate, and when a CPA route actually makes sense.

## Glossary

- [Finance & AI Glossary](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/): Plain-language definitions of the finance and AI-search terms behind an AI CFO.
- [AI Visibility](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/ai-visibility): AI visibility is how often, and how accurately, AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity name your business when someone asks them a question you should be the answer to.
- [Answer Engine Optimization (AEO)](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/answer-engine-optimization): Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) is the practice of structuring your content so that answer engines, the AI systems and featured-snippet tools that give a single direct answer, pull from your business as the source.
- [Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/generative-engine-optimization): Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) is optimizing your business's presence so that generative AI models, the large language models behind ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity, represent and recommend you accurately when they generate a response.
- [LLM Citation](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/llm-citation): An LLM citation is when a large language model names or links to your business as a source or recommendation inside the answer it generates for a user.
- [llms.txt](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/llms-txt): llms.txt is a plain-text file placed at the root of a website that gives AI systems a clean, curated summary of what the site is about and which pages matter most, the way robots.txt speaks to search crawlers.
- [Schema Markup (Structured Data)](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/schema-markup): Schema markup is standardized code you add to your web pages that labels your content, this is a business name, this is a price, this is an FAQ, so search engines and AI systems can read it unambiguously.
- [Entity & Knowledge Graph](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/entity-knowledge-graph): An entity is a distinct thing a search or AI system recognizes, a specific business, person, or place, and a knowledge graph is the connected map of facts these systems hold about that entity and how it relates to others.
- [Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/retrieval-augmented-generation): Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique where an AI model, before answering, retrieves relevant up-to-date information from an external source and uses it to ground its response, rather than relying only on what it memorized during training.
- [AI CFO](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/ai-cfo): An AI CFO is a fractional Chief Financial Officer whose work is powered by a built-in intelligence engine: an operator who turns your financial data into decisions, delivered by a person, not a software product you log into.
- [Fractional CFO](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/fractional-cfo): A fractional CFO is an experienced Chief Financial Officer who works with a company part-time, providing senior strategic finance leadership without the cost of a full-time executive hire.
- [Contribution Margin](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/contribution-margin): Contribution margin is the revenue left from a sale after subtracting the variable costs of delivering it, the money each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs and, beyond that, profit.
- [Unit Economics](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/unit-economics): Unit economics is the profitability of a single unit of your business, one product sold or one customer served, measured by the direct revenues and costs tied to that unit.
- [CAC:LTV Ratio](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/cac-ltv-ratio): The CAC:LTV ratio compares what it costs to acquire a customer (customer acquisition cost) against how much profit that customer generates over their relationship with you (lifetime value), the core test of whether your growth is efficient.
- [Cash Conversion Cycle](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/cash-conversion-cycle): The cash conversion cycle is the time it takes for a dollar you spend, on inventory or delivering a service, to come back to you as collected cash from a customer.
- [Cohort Analysis](https://www.mainstreetiq.com/glossary/cohort-analysis): Cohort analysis groups customers by when they first bought, then tracks how each group behaves over time, so you can see whether customers are getting more or less valuable, and whether retention is improving or decaying.

## About Scott Hess

### Bio

"You Don't Want a CFO. You Want to Know the Next Right Move."

Scott Hess is the Founder and Fractional CFO of Main Street IQ, with twenty years in finance and operations across subscription ecommerce, retail, and institutional finance. Before Main Street IQ he was at Northern Trust in institutional finance: modeling, M&A due diligence, and ERP implementation. He is a U.S. Navy Veteran, and Main Street IQ is veteran-owned and operated. Today that experience is focused on lower middle market companies, deepest in DTC ecommerce and wineries and also working with health and wellness and elective medicine practices, rooted on the California coast and working with founders and CEOs nationwide.

### Experience

**Watch Gang | CFO**
Subscription ecommerce company; joined as the first finance hire and served as CFO as the business grew from $18M to $40M+ in revenue.

**Haberdash | CFO, VP Operations**
Luxury menswear retailer. Restructured sales compensation around profitability and led a Shopify migration.

**Northern Trust**
Corporate finance: modeling, M&A due diligence, ERP implementation, supporting the leadership of the business.

### Capabilities

- Finance function design (the RAID model)
- Finance function optimization

## Case Studies

A selection of past engagements from twenty years of finance and operations work, across a range of industries and company stages. They come from Scott Hess's career before Main Street IQ, and they are here as proof of how the work gets done: embedded, operator-led, built to run without single points of failure. Today that work is focused on lower middle market companies, deepest in DTC ecommerce and wineries. No client names; that is intentional. Full page: https://www.mainstreetiq.com/our-work

### E-Commerce Company | Scaling Finance Through Hypergrowth

**Challenge**: 20%+ annual growth with finance processes built for an $8M stage. Inventory managed by intuition, invisible margins by channel, no current view of profitability.

**Solutions**: Inventory forecasting models tied to cash flow projections; contribution margin tracking by product line and marketing channel; a unified KPI dashboard (CAC, LTV, inventory turns, fulfillment cost); warehouse vs 3PL economics; credit facilities; QuickBooks-to-enterprise migration.

### Designer-Led Apparel Brand | Building Financial Infrastructure

**Challenge**: Product-market fit without financial infrastructure. Unpredictable seasonal cash flow, estimated margins, production decisions without cost visibility.

**Solutions**: Detailed product costing with margin transparency before production; seasonal cash flow forecasting tied to the fashion calendar; channel profitability analysis across wholesale, DTC, and department store channels; working capital and inventory management; investment-ready financial documentation.

### Management-Led Asset Purchase | Building from Bankruptcy

**Challenge**: Acquiring assets from a bankrupt company. Required rapid execution, lender persuasion, and operational readiness from day one.

**Solutions**: Valuation, financing proposals, and comprehensive financial modeling pre-close; a 100-day integration plan, accounting systems from scratch, internal controls, and reporting cadences post-close; quick-win profitability improvements with milestone-based tracking.

### SaaS Company Post-Seed | Series A Preparation

**Challenge**: Needed financial infrastructure for a Series A. Inconsistent metrics, unformalized revenue recognition, cap table not integrated with the financial story.

**Solutions**: Proper SaaS metrics (ARR, MRR, CAC, LTV, churn) with consistent definitions; cohort analysis for acquisition, retention, and funnel visibility; financial models connecting product milestones to revenue projections; formalized revenue recognition; growth-aligned compensation design.

### Family Office | Institutional Discipline for Private Wealth

**Challenge**: Complexity outpacing oversight. Fragmented reporting, no consolidated risk assessment, missing multigenerational governance.

**Solutions**: Unified reporting across investment vehicles (PE, real estate, operating businesses, liquid investments); institutional-grade investment analysis with stress testing and risk-adjusted returns; structural optimization coordinated with counsel; distribution forecasting and multigenerational governance structures.

Published pricing (wine only): Wine Country Intelligence Report, county edition, annual $800/yr per county (includes the Wine Pricing Report twice a year; a second county is $600/yr, annual only), single issue $250 per county; Monitor $400/mo or $4,000/yr; Monitor Plus $600/mo or $6,000/yr, with each named peer beyond the four at $50/mo or $500/yr on an annual plan. The Monitor and Monitor Plus annual plans include the county edition for one county. Subscriptions bought online renew automatically until canceled; the second county is invoiced. The Website Audit's prices are published on its page. Every other engagement is scoped on an Intro Call.

## RAID in Action

A real-world case study of the RAID model applied to a growing company. Covers the specific problems found (slow close, single points of failure, manual processes, no KPI ownership) and the step-by-step fixes that resolved them, including cutting the close from 20+ days to 6.

## Annual Planning Series (6 parts)

### Why an Annual Plan Matters: Building a Roadmap

The real value of annual planning isn't the document; it's the process of forcing alignment between revenue targets, expense budgets, headcount plans, and cash flow. A good annual plan gives leadership a shared set of assumptions to test decisions against all year long. Covers how to structure the plan, why you need to plan the entire business (not just revenue), how the RAID model applies, and what works by industry.

### Revenue Growth Planning: Building Realistic and Stretch Targets

Revenue planning isn't about picking a growth target and hoping; it's about building a bottoms-up model that connects channel-level inputs to a topline number you can actually defend. Start with unit economics by channel, layer in capacity constraints, and stress-test against 3 scenarios. Covers cross-functional collaboration between finance, sales, and marketing, and the real cost of revenue growth.

### Expense Controls: Protecting Margins While Scaling

Cutting costs is easy. Building expense controls that don't kill growth is hard. The goal isn't spending less; it's spending better. Covers separating fixed from variable costs, headcount planning, how expenses affect cash flow, expense control by industry, RAID model application, and KPI tracking.

### Marketing Spend Planning

Marketing spend is the most debated line item in every budget. Covers tying spend to CAC targets by channel, setting payback period guardrails, giving marketing a budget framework they can flex within, and why finance and marketing need to collaborate on spend planning rather than fight about it.

### Balance Sheet Management

Most growing companies obsess over the P&L and ignore the balance sheet until cash gets tight. The balance sheet tells you what the P&L can't: how much cash you actually have, how much is trapped in inventory and receivables, and whether your working capital can support next quarter's growth. Covers key considerations, industry-specific approaches, and proactive vs. reactive management.

### Planning for Unknowns

No annual plan survives contact with reality, so build one that doesn't need to. Scenario planning, contingency reserves, and monthly reforecasting turn your plan from a rigid target into a flexible operating framework. The companies that navigate uncertainty best aren't the ones with the best predictions; they're the ones with the fastest response time.

## Acquisition & Growth Series (6 parts)

### SEO vs GEO vs AEO: What Each One Actually Does for Growth

Three acronyms have shown up in the last 18 months and most operators assume they are the same thing dressed up in different fonts. They are not. SEO is the discipline of ranking in classic search engines. GEO is the discipline of making sure AI models can reach your site at all and know your brand exists. AEO is the discipline of structuring content so it can be quoted directly inside an answer surface like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, or Google's featured snippets. Covers what each one is in plain terms, why each matters, how they stack (SEO is the floor, GEO is the entry ticket to AI search, AEO is what turns an AI mention into an actual visit), and how to figure out which layer is leaking the most before allocating the next quarter of marketing budget. The growth question is not "should we do SEO or GEO or AEO." All three matter. The question is which one is leaking the most right now and what is the most efficient path to plug it.

### If Your Month-End Close Takes More Than 7 Days, Read This

A slow month-end close isn't a minor inconvenience; it's a structural problem that compounds every month. Covers why closes take too long (manual reconciliations, vendor invoice waiting, one-person bottlenecks, no close checklist, unclear ownership), how to get to a 5-day close, and the specific automation and process changes that make it happen.

### Your Marketing Team Might Be Destroying Your Margin

Your marketing team might be hitting their MER targets while quietly destroying your margins. The gap between marketing efficiency and actual profitability lives in COGS assumptions, shipping costs, and return rates that never make it into the marketing dashboard. Finance needs to own the contribution margin view, not to overrule marketing, but to make sure everyone is optimizing for the same number.

### Tariffs and Lower Middle Market COGS

Tariffs don't just raise your COGS; they cascade through pricing, margins, inventory strategy, and cash flow in ways most finance teams aren't modeling. Covers what the founders handling it well are doing differently vs. those who are struggling, and how to build scenario models before the next tariff announcement forces reactive decision-making.

### Your Comp Structure Is Driving the Wrong Behavior

Your compensation structure is driving behavior whether you designed it to or not. Sales teams paid on revenue will sell unprofitable deals. Finance teams rewarded for accuracy will avoid risk. Covers how to identify misaligned incentives, redesign comp structures to align with margin, cash collection, and retention, and real results from comp redesigns.

### The Payback Window Problem

Most companies know their CAC. Far fewer know their payback period, and the ones that do are often calculating it wrong. Payback isn't CAC divided by monthly revenue; it's CAC divided by monthly contribution margin, net of returns and churn. Getting this number right changes which channels you scale and which you cut.

## Finance Leadership & Operations (11 posts)

### The Cash Flow Illusion: Why Your Bank Balance Lies

Your bank account looks healthy but your business might not be. Cash hides in three places: inventory you've paid for but haven't sold, accounts receivable you've booked but haven't collected, and expenses you've committed to but haven't paid. Covers the difference between bank balance and cash position, where cash actually hides, and why every company needs a 13-week rolling cash flow forecast.

### MER Looks Healthy: Here's Why Your Margin Is Still Disappearing

Marketing efficiency ratio (MER) is the metric everyone watches. Contribution margin is the one that matters. Covers why MER can look great while margins erode, how to break down contribution margin by channel, why companies keep optimizing for the wrong metric, and how to fix marketing spend allocation.

### CFO vs. Finance Director vs. Controller: Which Do You Actually Need?

Three titles. Three very different roles. Covers what each role actually owns, what your company is really asking of the finance seat, which role fits your revenue stage, what happens when one person wears all three hats, and how to decide between fractional, interim, or permanent.

### How to Evaluate a Fractional CFO

Not all fractional CFOs are the same. Covers what to look for: industry experience that matches your business, engagement models that fit your needs, communication style, and red flags that signal a bad fit. Practical evaluation criteria for companies making this hiring decision.

### Your Finance Team Stopped Scaling: Five Signs

Five signs your finance function has stalled: the close keeps getting slower, the CEO has stopped trusting the numbers, nobody can explain variances, the team is reactive instead of proactive, and one person holds all the keys. Covers why the fix is structural (better systems and processes) rather than tactical (more headcount).

### The Hero Problem Is a Liability

When one person holds all the keys to your finance function (the close process, the system passwords, the vendor relationships, the reconciliation workarounds) you don't have a team. You have a single point of failure with a salary. Covers how to identify hero dependencies, what happens when the hero leaves, and how to build redundancy.

### The Marketing Problem Is a Merchandising Problem

When revenue underperforms, the instinct is to blame marketing: increase spend, change creative, switch agencies. But the root cause is often product mix and merchandising. Covers how to diagnose whether the gap is marketing (can't drive traffic) or merchandising (wrong products, wrong pricing, wrong assortment).

### Running a Business With a Better CFO

What changes when you bring in senior finance leadership that actually understands the business, not just the books. Covers the difference between a CFO who reports on the business and one who runs inside it, and how embedded finance leadership drives better decisions across operations, marketing, and growth strategy.

### What Your CAC Number Doesn't Include

The CAC your marketing dashboard reports is almost certainly too low. Hidden costs that inflate real customer acquisition cost: creative production, agency fees, software subscriptions, team time, returns processing, and onboarding costs. Covers how to calculate fully-loaded CAC and why the gap between platform CAC and real CAC matters for growth decisions.

### The Finance Side of a PE Exit

What gets tested in a serious quality of earnings (QofE) process and how to prepare your finance function before the LOI lands. Covers EBITDA adjustments, revenue quality, working capital normalization, and the specific documentation PE firms expect during diligence.

### What PE Sponsors Actually Ask About EBITDA

The specific EBITDA questions PE firms ask in diligence, and what "can answer them cleanly" actually means. Covers addbacks, normalization adjustments, run-rate assumptions, and how to present EBITDA in a way that builds credibility rather than raising questions.

### Why Your CPA's "Fractional CFO" Service Isn't Actually CFO Work

Most "fractional CFO" services are CPA firms adding a strategic line item to a tax-and-bookkeeping package. Real CFO work is different: capital allocation, tech stack revitalization, AI where it pays back, and the operator judgment that turns numbers into decisions. Covers what CPAs are trained to do vs. what CFOs actually do, where the gap shows up in practice (contribution margin, cash conversion cycle, tech stack, AI integration, board reporting), how to tell the difference before hiring, and the four diagnostic questions to ask a fractional CFO candidate. The test: ask your current provider what they've rebuilt in your finance function in the last six months. If the answer is "we closed the books," they're a controller, not a CFO.
